title: 'I carry the weight of taking somebody's life everyday': Peterborough officer who killed armed suspect says more mental health supports needed, inquest hears
subtitle: The inquest into Billy Shea's police involved shooting death heard from 5 witnesses last week
article: The line was drawn in the sand.

An armed Billy Shea exited the stolen convertible, and police resorted to use of force. In Shea's case, it was deadly force. A gunshot wound to the 27-year-old's torso followed a two-week, drug-fuelled crime spree that was supposed to end in a suicide pact with his girlfriend.

"I carry the weight of taking somebody's life everyday," explained the Peterborough Police Service officer that discharged his rifle twice into the back of Shea and ended a 45-minute standoff with Shea and his girlfriend on the Highway 7/115 northbound off-ramp in Peterborough on July 23, 2019.
The officer was one of five witnesses to testify last week at the inquest into the death of Shea.

A jury made a total of 17 recommendations, including eight to the Peterborough Police Service, after hearing four days of evidence. The jury ruled Shea's death a homicide, but the coroner's inquest verdict carries no criminal or civil liability.

The officer, whose name is being withheld for privacy reasons, was cleared criminally by the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), with the police oversight body finding the officer was justified in his use of force.

According to the SIU, officers observed a stolen red Mustang convertible in Millbrook on the evening in question. A standoff began when Shea crashed the car on the off-ramp near The Parkway and Sir Sanford Fleming Drive intersection. Police, including OPP and city police, approached the car and an interaction ensued between them and Shea.
Wanted by the OPP's repeat offender parole enforcement (ROPE) squad, he was armed with a triple barrel shotgun, the inquest heard.
"It just unfolded so quickly. It was nothing like I'd ever seen before," the officer testified.

During his testimony, the officer described erratic and uncontrolled behaviour by the individuals in the car, including pointing the shotgun at themselves, and playing with the trigger. He said Shea mentioned several times that he was going to die either by shooting himself or police were going to have to shoot him. Further, he told the jury that the woman repeatedly wanted the firearm.
"She wanted possession of the firearm, screaming ,'point it at them, point it at them, shoot them,'" he explained. "Both of them appeared willing to let their lives go, for what I don't know."

According to the SIU, a message went over police radios to all officers present that there was a risk of crossfire due to the location of various officers around the subject car. The officer was designated to take the shot if Shea were to leave the car.
The officer testified he made his line in the sand clear to Shea, and officers on scene pleaded with the suspect not to leave the car armed.
"Mr. Shea understood what would happen if he tried to get out of the vehicle," the officer told the jury. "He put me in a position where I had to use lethal force."
The officer told the jury the situation was like a movie, and he relives it every day.
"It impacts my life every day," he said, holding back his emotions. "I can't sleep at night. Anxious. My chest is tight."

In closing, the officer told the jury he thinks it is stigma within police services, and emergency services as whole, that mental health is not a valid reason to be off work. He said there are programs out there, but police services can do more.
"There's so much more that can be done," he explained.

The jury recommended the Peterborough Police Service improve its mental health care policies and the scope of mental health care support services available to assist officers in addressing mental health challenges that arise because of engagement in traumatic events such as this.
Peterborough Police Service Staff Insp. Jamie Hartnett says the service has come a long way in ending stigma and adding mental health resources, but there's always room for improvement.
"We recognize we have to be better at a lot of stuff. Sometimes, and unfortunately, it takes some of these tragic incidents where that change happens," he explained.

Hartnett says through the collective bargaining agreement, there are funds set aside for members to get support. He says even if a member is maxed out on those, the service can cover an additional number of appointments if needed.
The service also has a peer-support group that connects other members with members with lived experiences.
"They connect people who have been struggling or have been involved in a critical incident," he said.
Recently, Hartnett says the service reached out to the Wounded Warrior Program.
"We're going to start utilizing them to come in and have conversations with some of our members," he said.
In the 2024 budget, Hartnett says the service will be asking for money to create an employee wellness and disability management co-ordinator.
"We recognize that we need to do better and we need to do more for our members that are off. We can't have them stay off too long and not have good contact with them," he explained.
"We don't want to forget them. We talk about employee wellness, and that is something we definitely want to get."
